title: Paper 1 Model Answer Buddhism: Full Walkthrough
summary: Paper 1 model answer Buddhism walkthrough: learn the 3 + 7 structure, manage five responses in 75 minutes, and write focused IB World Religions answers.
body_markdown:
A strong **Paper 1 model answer Buddhism** response does not try to display everything you know. It does something harder: it selects the knowledge that answers the precise stimulus question, then explains that knowledge through accurate Buddhist concepts.


For the established IB World Religions SL format, Paper 1 lasts **1 hour 15 minutes** . The paper offers nine stimulus-based questions, one for each introductory religious tradition. You answer **five 10-mark questions** , selecting at least one from each of the three sections. Each question is divided into a **3-mark part and a 7-mark part** , giving you roughly 15 minutes per complete response.


That timing changes how you should write. A polished miniature essay may feel impressive, but an unfinished fifth response is expensive. The goal is controlled completeness.


### Paper 1 Buddhism checklist


Before exploring the model answer, keep this compact checklist in mind:


- Read the command term before studying the stimulus.
- Identify three distinct points for the 3-mark task.
- Support the 7-mark explanation with accurate Buddhist terminology.
- Refer directly to the stimulus rather than writing a memorized Buddhism summary.
- Develop connections between teachings, practices and goals.
- Spend approximately 15 minutes on each 10-mark question.
- Leave a brief final moment to check that all five questions are complete.


Students who need to strengthen the underlying content can begin with the[IB World Religions resource hub](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions) and the syllabus-aligned[Buddhism revision notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-2-buddhism/notes) .


### Understanding the IB World Religions exam format


Paper 1 tests breadth. You are not being asked for the sustained argument expected in a long essay. Instead, you must interpret short stimulus material and make relevant religious knowledge work quickly.


Paper 1 feature What it means for your strategy


Time allowed 1 hour 15 minutes


Questions available Nine, arranged across three sections


Questions answered Five, with at least one selected from each section


Marks per question 10 marks


Question structure 3 marks + 7 marks


Approximate time per question 15 minutes


A sensible rhythm is **4 minutes for part (a), 10 minutes for part (b), and 1 minute for checking or moving between questions** .


Question selection matters too. Scan all nine options before committing. Select questions where you understand both the stimulus and the broader concept behind it. Recognizing a Buddhist term is useful, but it is not enough if you cannot explain its relationship to belief or practice.


### How to approach the 3-mark stimulus question


The shorter task commonly rewards three accurate and distinct identifications. Think in units. One clear teaching, feature or observation is one possible unit of credit.


If asked to identify three Buddhist teachings shown in a stimulus, do not bury them inside a long introductory paragraph. State each point directly, preferably in a short numbered list or three unmistakable sentences. Use specific language such as *dukkha* , *tanha* , *anicca* or the Noble Eightfold Path when the stimulus supports it.


A student carries an enormous stack of books toward a tiny answer box while another student points out that the question requested something smaller.


*Knowing more is valuable. Selecting what the question needs is exam technique.*


### How to build the 7-mark explanation


The 7-mark section needs developed explanation rather than a longer list. A reliable paragraph pattern is:


**Claim → Buddhist concept → connection to the stimulus → significance**


Suppose the stimulus describes a person who continually seeks possessions but remains dissatisfied. You could claim that the scenario illustrates *tanha* . You would then define *tanha* as craving, connect the person's repeated acquisition to the stimulus, and explain that craving perpetuates *dukkha* . The explanation earns its weight because it shows how the ideas fit together.


Three habits make these answers stronger.


### Define terms in context


Do not simply insert specialist vocabulary. Explain what each term contributes. For example, *dukkha* can include obvious pain, but it also expresses the deeper unsatisfactoriness of conditioned existence. The[key concepts of Buddhism notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-21-key-concepts-of-buddhism/notes) can help you distinguish concepts that are often compressed into oversimplified definitions.


### Move from belief to consequence


Explanation often becomes stronger when it connects doctrine with lived religion. If impermanence, or *anicca* , is important, what follows from recognizing it? A Buddhist may become less attached to possessions, status or experiences because none provides permanent satisfaction.


Depending on the question, you might connect teachings to meditation, ethical conduct, chanting or other practices. The[Buddhist rituals study notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-22-rituals-in-buddhism/notes) and[religious experience in Buddhism notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-25-religious-experience-in-buddhism/notes) support this transition from abstract knowledge to religious life.


### Avoid claiming that all Buddhists are identical


Buddhism includes multiple traditions, communities and interpretations. Unless the question calls for a particular school, cautious phrases such as “many Buddhists” or “within Buddhist teaching” are often more accurate than universal claims. Precision is not hesitation. It is evidence that you understand religious diversity.


### Short Paper 1 model answer Buddhism walkthrough


The following is an original practice stimulus created for this walkthrough. It is not an official IB question.


> A person obtains everything they desire, yet each satisfaction soon fades. Recognizing this pattern, they begin to examine their cravings and follow a path of ethical conduct, mental discipline and wisdom.


**Part (a): Identify three Buddhist teachings reflected in the stimulus. \[3\]**


### Model response for 3 marks


1. Craving, or *tanha* , is connected with dissatisfaction.
2. Satisfaction is impermanent, reflecting the teaching of *anicca* .
3. The Noble Eightfold Path provides a way toward the cessation of *dukkha* .


**Part (b): Explain how the teachings reflected in the stimulus relate to the Buddhist path toward liberation. \[7\]**


### Model response for 7 marks


The stimulus reflects the Four Noble Truths because the person's repeated dissatisfaction illustrates *dukkha* , while their continuing desire reflects *tanha* , the craving associated with its arising. Although the person gains what they want, the satisfaction fades. This also demonstrates *anicca* , since pleasurable experiences and possessions are impermanent and therefore cannot provide lasting fulfilment.


The person begins to examine craving rather than pursuing it automatically. This reflects the Buddhist aim of understanding the causes of *dukkha* so that attachment can be reduced. The reference to ethical conduct, mental discipline and wisdom points toward the Noble Eightfold Path. Its practices are commonly grouped into these three areas and provide a practical response to the human problem identified by the Four Noble Truths.


Through wisdom, a practitioner develops clearer understanding of reality. Ethical conduct reduces actions rooted in greed, hatred and delusion, while mental discipline develops awareness and concentration. Together, these practices can weaken craving and ignorance. The stimulus therefore presents liberation not as another temporary possession, but as transformation through insight and disciplined practice.


### Common mistakes in Paper 1 stimulus questions


The first mistake is **retelling the stimulus** . Paraphrasing proves that you read it, but marks depend on identifying and explaining its religious meaning.


The second is **name-dropping terminology** . A paragraph containing *dukkha* , *anicca* , *anatta* and *nirvana* is not automatically strong. Every term needs a clear role in the explanation.


The third is **turning 3 marks into an essay** . Three visible points are usually more effective than a page of overlapping description.


The fourth is **writing only from memory** . Stimulus questions require interaction with the material provided. Quote or paraphrase a relevant detail, identify its doctrinal meaning, and explain why the connection matters.


The fifth is **using a single Buddhism template for every prompt** . A question about sacred texts needs different evidence from one about ritual or religious experience. Review the[introduction to Buddhism notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-13-buddhism-an-introduction/notes) , then use resources such as the[Buddhist sacred texts flashcards](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-23-sacred-texts-of-buddhism/flashcards) to make recall more flexible.


### A practical way to prepare


Build preparation around three layers.


First, learn concise definitions with RevisionDojo Study Notes and Flashcards. Second, apply those concepts to unfamiliar extracts through the Questionbank. Third, submit written responses to Grading tools or discuss weaknesses with AI Chat. The sequence matters: knowledge comes first, application follows, and feedback corrects what practice alone may leave invisible.


Closer to the exam, use Predicted Papers and Mock Exams under timed conditions. Review errors by category: missing knowledge, weak stimulus use, incomplete explanation or poor timing. The Coursework Library can show how careful religious studies writing handles evidence and terminology, while RevisionDojo Tutors can help when the same conceptual weakness keeps returning.


RevisionDojo works best as a connected system rather than a collection of isolated tools. A model answer shows the destination. Deliberate practice teaches you how to reach it within 15 minutes.


### Final takeaway


Paper 1 rewards disciplined selection. For Buddhism, that means identifying precise teachings in the 3-mark response, then explaining their relationships and significance in the 7-mark response. Keep the stimulus visible, connect doctrine to practice, and control your time across all five answers.


The quiet advantage is not memorizing the largest number of facts. It is knowing which fact belongs in this answer, in this paragraph, for this command term. RevisionDojo gives IB World Religions SL students the notes, retrieval practice, exam-style questions and feedback needed to develop that judgment.
